- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.3) or negative (≤-0.3) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast peak by 2–5% relative to prior high.
- After a sharp price spike (≥5% from prior 5-day avg), model often overshoots and fails to correct — cap forecast at +3% above peak or align with 30-day moving average.
- If sentiment is positive (≥0.6) and price is rising, model tends to overestimate — apply downward bias of 1–3% for next 3–5 days.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.3–0.6), model often underestimates — add 1–2% to forecast for next 5–7 days.
- Model consistently underestimates in early horizon (first 5–7 days) when sentiment is volatile — add 0.5–1.5% to forecast for first 5 days.
- If sentiment is negative and price is falling, model often fails to recognize trend reversal — adjust forecast to align with 10-day moving average or 30-day trend.
- Model tends to overestimate in high-sentiment periods (sentiment >0.7) — reduce forecast by 1–2% for next 3–5 days if sentiment remains high.
- When sentiment is low and price is near support, model often ignores support — add 0.5–1.5% to forecast to avoid undershoot.
- Model often fails to capture sentiment-driven mean reversion — if sentiment shifts from positive to negative, reduce forecast by 1–3% for next 3–5 days.
- In low-sentiment periods, model tends to overestimate — apply downward bias of 1–3% for next 5–7 days.
